title: When the House Sings
premise: Vesper Ravensworth, a pest controller who prides herself on rationality, is hired to clear an infestation at Hollowmere House just as a demolition crew unearths a cellar door sealed from the inside. The 'pests' leave fingerprints, then words, then memories that aren't hers, and Vesper realizes the house has been keeping something alive since 1974 by feeding on the town's forgotten dead. To survive, she must return what was taken—a child's remains the last resident, Edith Marlowe, buried beneath her own name—and convince dying Edith to sign the house back to the dead before the demolition erases every trace of them. In the end, Vesper signs as witness, the house exhales its final song, and she walks out carrying a memory of a sister she never had.
about_author: J. M. Eastwick is the pen name of a former building surveyor who spent a decade inspecting condemned properties across northern England and never once went into a basement without checking the ceiling first. Their fiction has appeared in several small-press anthologies, and they still keep a crowbar by the front door.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Vesper Ravensworth takes a routine pest contract at Hollowmere House, scheduled for demolition in three weeks, and finds droppings arranged in neat concentric circles. Her POV establishes her stubborn disbelief and financial desperation. Emotional beat: unease masked as professional boredom.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV: the grease smears along the pantry wall are unmistakably fingerprints—hundreds, overlapping, climbing toward the ceiling. She photographs everything for the report she'll never file. Emotional beat: the first crack in her certainty, dismissed with dark humor.

chapters.title: Edith Marlowe Signs Nothing
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Edith, 91, the last resident, refusing the developer's final purchase papers from her care home bed. She hums a tune no one taught her and tells her nurse the house is 'holding its breath.' Emotional beat: dread wrapped in defiance; we learn she hasn't left the grounds since 1974.

chapters.title: What the Excavator Found
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV: the demolition crew unearths a cellar door bolted from the inside, behind it a sealed room with fresh air and a child's shoe. The foreman quits on the spot. Emotional beat: vertigo—the impossible made physical, and Vesper's rational explanations start costing effort.

chapters.title: The Song in the Pipes
chapters.summary: Working alone at dusk, Vesper hears humming through the plumbing—the same tune Edith sings. She records it; playback reveals a second voice underneath, a child's. Emotional beat: loneliness curdling into companionship-with-something, which frightens her more than menace would.

Interleaved archival fragments and Edith's POV: a summer when her younger sister Winnie vanished, when the town quietly stopped speaking of the Marlowes, when Edith began sealing doors. Emotional beat: grief fossilized into ritual; the reader understands before Vesper does.

chapters.title: Infestation Protocol
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV: she deploys traps, poison, cameras. By morning the traps hold wildflowers, the poison is gone, and the camera shows her own sleeping face filmed from the corner of the room. Emotional beat: humiliation tipping into terror—she is being studied back.

chapters.title: Staying Invisible
chapters.summary: Vesper researches Hollowmere's history and finds every prior pest controller listed in parish records died within a year, unmourned. The house only keeps those no one would miss. Emotional beat: the theme lands—her invisibility, her lifelong armor, is exactly what makes her prey.

chapters.title: The Tenant Below
chapters.summary: Vesper descends to the sealed door and speaks through it. Something answers in her mother's voice, then in her own childhood voice, recounting memories she never told anyone. Emotional beat: seduction—the house offers belonging, and part of her wants it.

chapters.title: Winnie's Room
chapters.summary: Behind a plastered-over wall Vesper finds a child's bedroom preserved since 1974, drawings on the wallpaper depicting the house itself with a small figure inside the walls. Edith's POV closes the chapter: she knows Vesper has found it. Emotional beat: tenderness turned claustrophobic.

chapters.title: The Developer's Men
chapters.summary: Two crew members break in overnight to strip copper piping; Vesper finds one catatonic, humming, his eyes tracking something across the ceiling, the other simply gone. Emotional beat: stakes made flesh—the house doesn't want her gone anymore, it wants witnesses removed.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: In the county archive, Vesper matches the child's shoe to Winnie Marlowe, declared runaway in 1974, and finds Edith's signed statement claiming Winnie 'went into the house.' Emotional beat: revelation reframing everything—Edith wasn't hiding a crime; she was honoring a bargain.

chapters.title: The Bargain
chapters.summary: Edith's POV, lucid at last: in 1974 the house offered to keep Winnie alive inside its walls if someone stayed to remember her. Edith paid fifty years of memory, feeding the house her own past until almost nothing remained. Emotional beat: devastating sympathy—the villain was a grieving sister all along.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Vesper realizes the house isn't holding Winnie hostage—it's holding her together, and the demolition will scatter her into nothing. The debt runs the other way: the living owe the dead a name. Emotional beat: Vesper's disbelief finally breaks, not into fear but into responsibility.

chapters.title: Convincing Edith
chapters.summary: Vesper brings the purchase papers to the care home and asks Edith to sign the house over—not to the developer, but formally, legally, to Winnie. Edith refuses: signing means forgetting Winnie entirely. Emotional beat: the cruelest choice—peace purchased with the last of a memory.

chapters.title: The House Objects
chapters.summary: That night Hollowmere fights back: doors seal, the song becomes a scream, and Vesper is trapped inside while the walls show her the belonging she could have—a whole family of the forgotten, herself included. Emotional beat: temptation at maximum; the house makes a genuinely good offer.

chapters.title: What Vester Can't Remember
chapters.summary: Trapped, Vesper discovers pages of her own handwriting she never wrote, describing a sister. The house has already begun editing her, inserting Winnie-shaped holes into her life. Emotional beat: horror of self-erasure—survival now means refusing comfort.

chapters.title: Signing
chapters.summary: Vesper escapes at dawn, reaches Edith, and makes the argument that saves them both: a name written down outlives the one who writes it. Edith signs the house to Winnie Marlowe, deceased, age nine, and whispers goodbye to a sister she can already feel slipping away. Emotional beat: grief and release in one stroke of the pen.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: With the deed transferred, the house's hunger ends. Edith dies peacefully that evening, humming the tune one final time, complete. Vesper's POV: the song in the pipes goes quiet mid-verse, like a held breath released. Emotional beat: mourning that feels like mercy.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: The crew razes Hollowmere without incident; the sealed door opens easily now onto an empty room with wildflowers on the floor. Vesper supervises, unpaid, making sure every timber is handled gently. Emotional beat: funeral as labor; the price of survival paid forward.

chapters.title: A Memory of a Sister
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Vesper finds the forged pages in her own files and chooses not to burn them. She visits the vacant lot, leaves wildflowers, and says Winnie's name aloud—the first mourner the girl ever had besides Edith. Emotional beat: belonging chosen rather than imposed.

chapters.title: When the House Sings
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Vesper's POV: she takes a call about another property, another infestation, and this time she listens before she discounts. Somewhere far off, faintly, something hums. She writes down the tune so it won't be lost. Emotional beat: quiet resolution—belief as an act of remembrance, and vigilance as inheritance.
